unit-lc1.title: The Lemonade Crime · Ch. 1–5: The Accusation
unit-lc1.srcName: The Lemonade Crime, chapters 1–5 (full text in Drive)
unit-lc1.source: The Lemonade Crime (Jacqueline Davies), reading companion 1 of 3

summary.text: The opening of The Lemonade Crime, chapters 1–5 (Fraud through Accused): Evan and Jessie Treski start fourth grade in the same class, Evan is certain Scott Spencer stole the $208 he earned in last summer's lemonade war at Jack's pool party, and Jessie — who believes in rules the way other people believe in weather — serves Scott with a homemade warrant and sets a trial for Friday. Every chapter opens with a real legal term and its definition.

why.text: This book does something sneaky: it teaches real courtroom ideas — evidence, hearsay, the accused, making amends — through a playground fight over stolen lemonade money. The table of contents is a map of a trial. If you learn each chapter's legal word as you go, you will finish the book knowing how fairness actually works, not just how it feels.

objectives.text: Define the five legal terms the opening chapters are named for: fraud, revenge, eyewitness, hearsay, accused — the book's own definitions.
Tell the difference between being certain someone did something and having proof they did.
Apply Megan's test to any story: did the teller see it with their own eyes, or is it a rumor?
Explain what each side risks under the Agreement of Atonement, and why signed stakes make the trial real.
Use the table of contents to predict where the story is headed.

parentNote.text: Rebuilt from the complete chapters 1–5 you uploaded to Drive — this replaces the earlier draft built from sample pages (same unit id, so checking the library swaps it in; nothing to clean up). All five chapter definitions are now quoted verbatim, including eyewitness and hearsay, which were previously my paraphrases marked as study suggestions. The new material carries the strongest moment in the opening: Evan realizing he never actually saw Scott take the money, yet he told everyone Scott did — which makes his own story exactly the hearsay chapter 4 defines. That, plus Megan's 'did you see it yourself?' test and the mother's line about rumors and pigeons, is the dinner conversation. Two analysis questions (rules vs. fairness, certainty vs. proof) are my framing and marked as study suggestions.

nextUp.text: Read through chapter 5 first. Then cards once, and a couple of quiz rounds.

cards.def:
**Fourth grader, big brother, the wronged party — his $208 is gone.**
• Earned every dollar in last summer's lemonade war; it vanished at Jack's pool party.
• Best basketball player in the grade, in Jessie's opinion — and he 'thought with his whole body, not just his brain.'
• Watch the gap between what Evan KNOWS and what he can PROVE.
cards.hint: Evan's problem isn't just the money. It's that nobody can prove anything.

cards.def:
**Evan's younger sister — she skipped third grade, so it's the fourth day of fourth grade for both of them.**
• Youngest in the class: no bike license yet, still walked to school by her mom.
• Rules and fairness are her native language; people and 'those looks' are the foreign one.
• Her answer to an unfair world: run it like a courtroom.
cards.hint: Jessie doesn't get mad at unfairness. She organizes against it.

cards.def:
**The accused — and, in Jessie's opinion, 'a faker and a fraud' long before the Xbox.**
• Cut the heads off the art-room daffodils; erased stars so his desk group would win the Team Award; never got caught.
• Brags, cheats at Go Fish, keeps the snacks at his house locked in a metal file cabinet.
• None of that is proof he took the $208. That's the uncomfortable part.
cards.hint: Being unpopular isn't evidence. That's sort of the whole point.

cards.def:
**Jessie's friend — and the sharpest thinker about rumors in the book so far.**
• Her test for any story: 'Did you see him take the money or the candy bar?'
• 'I don't listen to rumors. People probably say things about me that aren't true. And about you, too.'
cards.hint: Megan is the friend who comes along AND asks the honest question.

cards.def:
**The whole case in one number.**
• During the heat wave, the boys swam at Jack's; Evan's shorts — money in the pocket — lay folded on the bed in Jack's bedroom.
• Scott left the pool for the bathroom, then ran out of the house saying he had to go home right away. When Evan went in to get dressed, the money was gone.
• Opportunity and timing point one way. But nobody SAW anything.
cards.hint: Keep asking: where is the money RIGHT NOW? The book knows you're wondering.

cards.def:
**The teacher — she runs 4-O with an African shekere, a rubber chicken, and firm calm.**
• Class jobs rotate weekly, from Paper Collector and Equipment Manager to Chicken Dresser and Goofy Face Maker.
• When Jessie asks what the Xbox cost: 'We don't ask each other how much things cost. It isn't polite.'
cards.hint: The classroom has its own rules of order — a small courtroom before the real one.

cards.def:
**Jessie's note lights the fuse: 'Scott Spencer got an Xbox 20/20. Where do you think he got the money for that???'**
• Slipped into Evan's hand on his way past her desk.
• One sentence of fact, one question of suspicion — and Evan crushes it in his fist.
cards.hint: Three question marks. Jessie already knows what answer she expects.

cards.def:
**The newest game system — surround-sight goggles, motion-sensing gloves — and you can't buy it in a store yet.**
• Scott's explanation: 'My mom knows people in Japan.' And later: 'I did a lot of chores around the house.'
• When Evan asks 'Who bought it? You or your parents?' Scott answers, 'I did. All my own money.'
• That answer is why there's going to be a trial.
cards.hint: The price of the Xbox is the exact shape of the hole in Evan's pocket.

cards.def:
**The crime of deceiving someone for personal or financial gain; a person who pretends to be something he or she is not.**
• That's the book's own definition, word for word, at the top of chapter 1.
• Two meanings: the trick, and the person doing the tricking.
cards.hint: A fraud lies to GET something — money, credit, a reputation.

cards.def:
**The act of causing pain or harm to another person because that person has injured you in some way.**
• Chapter 2's definition, verbatim — and its last line is 'Evan wanted revenge.'
• Notice what revenge is not: it is not getting the money back, and it is not fairness.
cards.hint: Revenge answers harm with harm. Justice answers harm with repair.

cards.def:
**A person who actually sees something happen and so can give a first-person account of the event.**
• Chapter 3's definition, verbatim.
• Jessie's wish, watching the boys doubt Scott's chore story: 'If only there'd been an eyewitness — like the crime shows on TV.' There wasn't one.
cards.hint: Eye + witness: the eyes have to have been there.

cards.def:
**Quoting someone else's words when that person is not present to say whether those words are true; rumor.**
• Chapter 4's definition, verbatim — and it adds: 'Hearsay is not allowed as evidence in a court of law.'
• Hearsay can be true. The problem is nobody can check it.
cards.hint: HEAR-say: it reached your ears, not your eyes.

cards.def:
**A person who has been charged with a crime or who is on trial for a crime.**
• Chapter 5's definition, verbatim.
• Being the accused is a position, not a verdict — the trial hasn't happened yet.
cards.hint: Accused means charged, not guilty. Courts exist for the space between.

cards.def:
**Jessie serves Scott a homemade 'Warrant for the Arrest of Scott Spencer,' written with her grandmother's calligraphy pen.**
• The charge: stealing $208 from the pocket of Evan Treski's shorts on September 5th. Court date: Friday.
• Her rule: once Scott grabbed the paper — 'You touched it. That means you've been served.'
• She learned it all from 'Trial by Jury: The American Legal System in a Nutshell,' a booklet her mom wrote for work.
cards.hint: Jessie read one booklet and built a working legal system from it.

cards.def:
**The signed deal that makes the trial real — Evan, Jessie and Scott all sign.**
• If GUILTY: Scott gives his Xbox 20/20 to Evan, to keep forever.
• If NOT GUILTY: Evan and Jessie stand up in Morning Meeting and tell the whole class they lied, then apologize.
• Both sides now have something to lose. That's what makes Friday matter.
cards.hint: Atonement means making up for a wrong — whoever loses, someone owes it.

cards.term: Chapter titles = a trial, in order
cards.def:
**The table of contents is a courtroom map: Fraud → Revenge → Eyewitness → Hearsay → Accused → Impartial → Due Diligence → Defense → Bona Fide → Trial by Jury → Perjury → Sixth Amendment → Circumstantial Evidence → Fighting Words → Balance → Amends.**
• The story will walk the whole path of a real case.
• Last stop: Amends — making things right, not just winning.
cards.hint: The contents page is the biggest spoiler-free prediction tool you'll ever get.

cards.def:
**Evan is completely sure. He can't prove anything. Those are different problems.**
• Certainty is a feeling inside one person.
• Proof is something other people can check for themselves.
• The whole trial exists to bridge that gap — or expose it.
cards.hint: The more someone says 'I just KNOW', the more this book wants you to ask 'how?'

cards.def:
**'Rumors are like pigeons. They fly everywhere and make a mess wherever they go.' — Evan's mom**
• Evan remembers this line right after an uncomfortable realization: he never SAW Scott take the money, but he told everyone Scott did.
• The line is true in both directions — even about rumors you believe.
cards.hint: Whose rumor is flying around the fourth grade right now? Check who released it.

cards.def:
**The legend of 4-O: peach pits on his dresser, a box of old shoelaces, and — supposedly — an envelope of his own toenail clippings.**
• 'At least, that's what everybody said, though Jessie was pretty sure that no one had actually seen the envelope.'
• Read that sentence again. It's hearsay — and even Jessie half believes it. The book is quietly testing you.
cards.hint: Even the joke character is a lesson about rumors, if you catch it.

cards.term: Ponder: what should happen to Scott?
cards.def:
**Everyone is sure Scott did it. Nobody saw him do it.**
• Before reading on: what would be FAIR to do next — and who gets to decide?
• Ask this one at dinner. Watch how different the answers are.
cards.hint: No wrong answers. But notice whether your answer needs proof or just certainty.

cards.def:
**Mid-scene, Jessie realizes she should have talked to Evan before serving the warrant.**
• It was his money, his fight, his friends — he has to face these boys at recess every day, and he'll have to testify.
• Was serving the warrant brave, or was it taking over something that wasn't hers? Could it be both?
cards.hint: Good intentions can still skip the most important question: did you ask?

cards.def:
**The book ends on making-things-right, not on winning.**
• Prediction: how does this end — punishment, payback, or something harder than both?
• Write your guess down and check it at the finish.
cards.hint: Titles keep promises. This one is promising something about the ending.

questions.passage: fraud (frôd), n. The crime of deceiving someone for personal or financial gain; a person who pretends to be something that he or she is not.
questions.q: Using the book's own definition, which of these is fraud?
opts: A kid who accidentally gives back the wrong change
A kid who asks to borrow five dollars
A kid selling 'magic' rocks, claiming they grant wishes, for $5 each
A kid selling lemonade cheaper than the stand next door
questions.hint: Fraud needs two parts: deception, and something gained by it.
steps: Pull the two requirements out of the definition: deceiving someone + doing it for gain.
Test each option: wrong change is a mistake (no deceiving on purpose); borrowing is honest; underselling is just competition.
The magic rocks are a lie told to collect $5 — deception, for gain. That is fraud by the book's exact definition.

ex.main: **The magic rocks.** Fraud = a lie with a payday. Mistakes, requests and competition all lack the deliberate deception.
ex.tip: When a definition is quoted, grade every option against its exact parts — the wrong answers usually fail one specific word.

questions.passage: "Fine," said Evan, taking out one cookie and putting it back in the cookie jar. "Three for you. Three for me. Happy?"
questions.q: The book opens with Evan and Jessie splitting cookies exactly evenly. Why start there?
opts: It shows this family keeps careful score — fairness is the house language, and this whole book is about fairness
It shows Evan and Jessie are not speaking to each other
It shows Evan always takes more than his share
It shows Jessie doesn't actually care about the cookies
questions.hint: First scenes are promises. What is this one promising the book will be about?
steps: Look at what actually happens: Jessie calls 'no fair', Evan recounts, they land on three-and-three.
Jessie even corrects him: 'It's not about being happy. It's about being fair.' She says the theme out loud on page one.
Now zoom out: a book that opens with an exactly-fair split is announcing its subject — what fairness costs and how you get it.
That is why chapter 1 is called Fraud: the fair-split family is about to meet someone who doesn't play by split rules.

ex.main: **It plants fairness as the family language.** Authors spend page one carefully. Jessie's own line — 'It's about being fair' — is the book's whole subject in five words.
ex.tip: When a small scene opens a book, ask what bigger thing it rehearses. Openings are rarely about the cookies.

questions.passage: revenge (ri-věnj′), n. The act of causing pain or harm to another person because that person has injured you in some way.
questions.q: By this definition, which response to a stolen bike is REVENGE?
opts: Reporting it to the school office
Asking the kid to give it back
Holding a fair hearing about who took it
Scratching up the bike of the kid you think took yours
questions.hint: Revenge answers harm with harm — no referee involved.
steps: The definition's key parts: causing pain or harm, because they harmed you first.
Reporting, asking, and holding a hearing all aim at fixing the wrong — none of them injure anyone.
Scratching the other bike creates new harm as payback. That is revenge, exactly as defined.
Chapter 2 ends with 'Evan wanted revenge' — hold onto this definition and watch which road he actually takes.

ex.main: **Scratching the other kid's bike.** Revenge manufactures new harm; the other three options try to repair the old one. Chapter 2 ends by putting Evan at exactly this fork.
ex.tip: Revenge vs. justice questions come down to one test: does the response repair harm, or manufacture more of it?

questions.q: Where was Evan's $208 when it disappeared?
opts: In the pocket of his shorts, folded on the bed in Jack's bedroom while the boys swam
In his desk at school
In the cash box at the lemonade stand
In his backpack on the school bus
questions.hint: Heat wave. Pool basketball. Everyone in the water — almost everyone.
steps: Chapter 2 lays out the scene: last week, mid heat wave, at Jack's house, all the boys playing pool basketball.
Evan left his shorts folded on the bed in Jack's bedroom — with the $208 in the pocket.
Scott got out of the pool for the bathroom, then suddenly ran out of the house saying he had to go home.
When Evan went in to get dressed, the money was gone. That timing is the whole case against Scott.

ex.main: **In his shorts on Jack's bed.** The details matter: the money was unguarded, and exactly one person left the pool during that window. Suspicious — and still not the same thing as seen.
ex.tip: In mystery-shaped books, pin down the where and when of the loss first. Every argument afterward leans on it.

questions.q: Put the story so far in order.
opts: Last summer's lemonade war leaves Evan with $208
The money disappears at Jack's pool party
Jessie's note about the Xbox turns Evan's suspicion into fury
Jessie serves Scott a warrant and the trial is set for Friday
questions.hint: Money earned, money gone, the note, then Jessie's kind of answer.
steps: The lemonade war is the prequel — it is where the $208 came from, before this book begins.
Then the pool party: the money vanishes during pool basketball at Jack's.
At school, Scott shows off his Xbox 20/20 and Jessie slips Evan the note — 'Where do you think he got the money for that???'
And because this family speaks fairness, the answer isn't a punch — it is a warrant, a signed agreement, and a court date on Friday.

ex.main: **War → pool party → the note → the warrant.** Earn, lose, rage, organize. Each step follows from the one before — and the chapter titles predicted all of it.
ex.tip: The order of events in a mystery is itself evidence. Get the timeline straight before judging anyone in it.

questions.q: Jessie calls Megan at 7:00, 7:30, 7:55 AND 8:10 to make sure they get to school on time. What does that show about Jessie?
opts: She is forgetful and keeps losing track
When something matters to her, she cannot let it go — she manages it minute by minute
She secretly dislikes Megan
She is usually the one running late
questions.hint: Four calls before 8:15 is not an accident. It's a personality.
steps: Count the calls: four, spaced tighter as the deadline nears — that is monitoring, not forgetting.
Megan's grumble ('I was late because you kept calling me') confirms it landed as pressure.
This is the same Jessie who wrote a warrant in calligraphy the night before: intense, systematic, unable to leave an important thing alone.
The book shows you her character in a phone log before the big scene needs it.

ex.main: **She can't let go of what matters.** Four calls in seventy minutes is Jessie's engine on display — the same engine that built the courtroom.
ex.tip: Small habits are character evidence. Authors plant them early so the big actions later feel inevitable.

questions.passage: accused (ə-kyoozd′), n. A person who has been charged with a crime or who is on trial for a crime.
questions.q: According to this definition, being 'the accused' means:
opts: You have been proven guilty
You saw the crime happen
You have been charged — the trial hasn't decided anything yet
You are the person who was harmed
questions.hint: Charged and guilty are two different words on purpose.
steps: Read the definition closely: charged with a crime, or on trial for one.
Neither of those words means guilty — a verdict is what a trial produces at the END.
So the accused stands in the space between suspicion and judgment. As of chapter 5, that is Scott's address.
This is the word the whole book turns on: what do we owe someone who is accused but not proven?

ex.main: **Charged, not judged.** Accused is a position in a process, not an outcome. The book names chapter 5 for it right as the playground starts forgetting the difference.
ex.tip: Legal words are precise on purpose. When the book bolds a definition, expect the plot to test exactly that precision.

questions.passage: eyewitness (ī′wĭt′nĭs), n. A person who actually sees something happen and so can give a first-person account of the event.
questions.q: Listening to the boys doubt Scott's chore story, Jessie wishes there had been an eyewitness at the pool party. Why would one eyewitness change everything?
opts: Because an eyewitness would have to be an adult
Because someone who actually saw it could give a first-person account that others can question and check
Because eyewitnesses are never wrong
Because Scott would confess the moment someone claimed to have seen him
questions.hint: What does the definition say an eyewitness can give that nobody at the pool party can?
steps: Take the definition apart: actually sees it happen → can give a first-person account.
Compare that to what the fourth grade has now: everyone is SURE, but every story traces back to Evan's suspicion, not to anyone's eyes.
An eyewitness isn't automatically right — but their account can be questioned, tested and checked, which a feeling cannot.
That is why Jessie wishes for one 'like the crime shows on TV': without an eyewitness, her case is all certainty and no evidence.

ex.main: **A first-person account others can check.** The definition is the answer: seeing it yourself is what turns a story into evidence. Nobody at Jack's house saw anything — which is the hole in the middle of the whole case.
ex.tip: When a chapter opens with a definition, the chapter usually shows you the definition's ABSENCE. Ask what's missing, not just what's there.

questions.passage: "Did you see him take the money or the candy bar?" she asked. Evan shook his head. "No, but Ryan said—" "That's just a rumor, then," said Megan.
questions.q: What test is Megan applying to Evan's stories about Scott?
opts: Whether the story is interesting enough to be worth repeating
Whether Scott has done other bad things before
Whether most of the class already believes the story
Whether the teller saw it with their own eyes — anything secondhand is just a rumor
questions.hint: Her question is about Evan's eyes, not about Scott's character.
steps: Look at what Megan actually asks: not 'is Scott the kind of kid who steals?' but 'did YOU SEE him take it?'
Evan's answer starts 'No, but Ryan said—' and she stops him right there: secondhand, so it's a rumor.
That is chapter 3 and chapter 4 compressed into one playground question: eyewitness or hearsay, seen or heard.
Notice she applies it evenly — 'People probably say things about me that aren't true. And about you, too.' The test protects everyone, including people you don't like.

ex.main: **Seen with your own eyes, or it's a rumor.** Megan runs the exact test a real court runs on evidence — and she's the only kid in the book applying it to a story she'd rather believe.
ex.tip: The hardest place to apply the rumor test is to a story you already agree with. That's also where it matters most.

questions.passage: Rumors are like pigeons. They fly everywhere and make a mess wherever they go.
questions.q: Evan remembers his mother saying this. What does the comparison mean?
opts: Rumors travel on their own, land everywhere, and leave damage someone else has to clean up
Rumors are harmless background noise, like birds in a city
Rumors always fly home to the person who started them
Rumors disappear if you stop feeding them
questions.hint: Two parts to the pigeon: where it goes, and what it leaves behind.
steps: Unpack the two halves of the comparison: pigeons 'fly everywhere' — nobody steers them once they're loose.
And they 'make a mess wherever they go' — the damage lands on whoever happens to be underneath.
Apply it to the story: the Scott-stole-it rumor is already loose in the fourth grade, flying from kid to kid without anyone checking it.
The timing of the memory is the point: Evan recalls the line right after realizing HE is the one who released this particular pigeon.

ex.main: **Rumors spread uncontrollably and leave damage behind.** The comparison has teeth because Evan remembers it at the worst possible moment — just as he realizes the biggest rumor flying around is his.
ex.tip: When a character remembers a saying mid-story, ask why the author chose THAT moment for the memory. Timing is meaning.

questions.q: In chapter 4, Megan's question leads Evan to an uncomfortable realization about the missing money. What is it?
opts: That Scott might quietly return the money
That Megan is the one who started the rumor
That he never actually saw Scott take the money — yet he told all his friends that Scott did
That the money was never in his shorts to begin with
questions.hint: Run Megan's test on Evan's own story. What happens?
steps: Megan asks whether Evan SAW any of the thefts he lists. He didn't — 'No, but Ryan said—'.
Then the book turns the light around: Evan never actually saw Scott take the $208 either.
But he 'had told everyone — Paul and Ryan and Adam and Jack — that Scott had taken it. And they'd all believed him.'

By the book's own chapter-4 definition, Evan's story reached everyone else as hearsay: they believe it because he said it, not because anyone saw it. He may still be right — but what's flying around the fourth grade is a rumor, and he released it.

ex.main: **He never saw it — and he spread it anyway.** This is the bravest move in the opening chapters: the book makes its hero the biggest source of hearsay in the story, while still letting him be possibly right.
ex.tip: Good books test their own hero with the book's own rules. When a definition appears at a chapter head, try applying it to the main character first.

questions.q: Evan is COMPLETELY certain Scott took the money. What is the difference between his certainty and actual proof?
opts: There is no difference if you're certain enough
Certainty is a feeling inside one person; proof is something other people can check for themselves
Proof is just certainty shared by more people
Certainty counts as proof if you were the victim
questions.hint: Which one could convince a fair stranger who wasn't there?
steps: Define each honestly: certainty lives inside Evan — nobody else can look at it.
Proof lives outside: a witness, the money found somewhere, something a stranger could examine.
Notice the trap in the other options: many people being certain is still just stacked feelings, and being the victim makes you the most certain and the least neutral at once.
The book's whole trial exists because the playground has maximum certainty and, so far, zero proof.

ex.main: **Certainty is private; proof is checkable.** Evan may even be RIGHT — and it still wouldn't make his feeling into evidence. That uncomfortable gap is the engine of the entire book.
ex.tip: This distinction shows up far beyond novels: every argument about who did what runs on it. Ask 'could a fair stranger verify this?'

questions.q: Put the warrant scene in order.
opts: Jessie writes the warrant at home with her grandmother's calligraphy pen
Scott grabs the paper and Jessie declares he's been served
Jessie reads the charge and the Xbox punishment out loud to the whole line
Scott names his counter-deal and Evan says 'Deal'
questions.hint: Prepare, serve, read, respond — the shape of the scene.
steps: The preparation happened before school: the warrant is already written, in calligraphy, when Jessie pulls it from her backpack.
Serving comes next — and by Jessie's rule, the moment Scott touches the paper, 'you've been served.'
Only then does she read it aloud: the charge, the Friday court date, and the punishment — the Xbox goes to Evan.
Scott answers with his own stakes: if he's found not guilty, Evan and Jessie apologize in front of everyone. Evan says 'Deal' — and now it's real.

ex.main: **Write → serve → read → deal.** The scene walks the real legal steps in order, which is exactly why it works — Jessie is running an actual procedure, not throwing a tantrum.
ex.tip: When a scene follows a formal procedure, use the procedure as your memory scaffold. The steps carry the story.

questions.q: The Agreement of Atonement sets the stakes for Friday's trial. What does each side risk?
opts: Guilty: Scott is suspended from school. Not guilty: nothing happens
Guilty: Scott returns the $208. Not guilty: Jessie pays Scott $208
Guilty: Scott apologizes at Morning Meeting. Not guilty: Evan gives Scott his basketball
Guilty: Scott gives his Xbox 20/20 to Evan forever. Not guilty: Evan and Jessie apologize to Scott in front of the whole class
questions.hint: One side risks the console. The other side risks their word, out loud, at Morning Meeting.
steps: Jessie's warrant names the punishment if guilty: the Xbox 20/20 goes to Evan Treski, to keep forever.
Scott's counter-deal names the other side: if he's found not guilty, Evan and Jessie stand up in Morning Meeting, admit they told lies, and apologize — in front of everyone, including Mrs. Overton.
Both sides sign the Agreement of Atonement. Notice the money itself isn't in the deal — the stakes are the Xbox and public honor.

ex.main: **Xbox forever vs. a public apology.** Interesting detail: neither outcome returns the $208. The trial is really about reputation — who gets believed — which tells you what this fight was about all along.
ex.tip: Look at what the stakes AREN'T. What's missing from a deal often says more than what's in it.

questions.q: Where did Jessie learn how trials, warrants and serving papers work?
opts: From watching her mother argue cases in court
From 'Trial by Jury: The American Legal System in a Nutshell' — a public-service booklet her mom wrote for work
From a social studies unit Mrs. Overton taught
From one of Evan's library books
questions.hint: Her mom isn't a lawyer — but she writes about the law for her job.
steps: Chapter 5 says Jessie had been reading a booklet called 'Trial by Jury: The American Legal System in a Nutshell.'
It's one of the public-service booklets her mom writes as a public relations consultant — writing ABOUT the law, not practicing it.
That's very Jessie: she didn't absorb the trial idea from TV drama. She studied a manual and followed the steps.

ex.main: **Her mom's booklet.** A nine-year-old ran a legally-shaped process off one pamphlet — 'served' by touch, warrant, court date. The book rewards her homework by making the procedure basically sound.
ex.tip: Where a character LEARNED something tells you how they'll use it. Manual-readers follow steps; TV-watchers copy scenes.

questions.q: In chapter 1, Jessie scolds Scott for cutting: 'The rule is you go to the end of the line.' In chapter 5, Jessie herself marches into the middle of the line to serve the warrant. What is the book showing you?
opts: For Jessie, rules serve fairness — and when the two collide, she picks fairness, even bending a rule she enforced on Scott
Jessie has stopped caring about rules completely
The school cancelled the line rule between chapters
Jessie forgot the rule she quoted earlier
questions.hint: She hasn't changed. Look at what the rules are FOR, in her mind.
steps: Line up the two scenes: same girl, same line, opposite behavior — that's deliberate authorial design, not a slip.
Ask what Jessie actually cares about in each scene: in chapter 1, the rule IS the fairness (no cutting). In chapter 5, following the line rule would delay what she sees as justice.
So the pattern is: rules are Jessie's tools for fairness, not her religion. When a rule blocks the mission, the mission wins.
File this away: a girl who bends rules for her own case will have opinions about courtroom rules later. Watch for it.

ex.main: **Rules are her tools for fairness — fairness comes first.** The mirrored line scenes are a quiet character study: Jessie isn't a rule-follower, she's a justice-seeker who usually finds rules useful.
ex.tip: When a book repeats a setting (the same line, twice), compare the scenes side by side. Repetition with a twist is how authors argue.

questions.passage: "There's no way you saved up that much money just from chores," said Adam.
questions.q: Why don't the boys buy Scott's explanation for the Xbox money?
opts: Because Scott never does any chores
Because Adam saw Scott take Evan's money
Because the amount doesn't fit the story — a console that expensive from 'chores,' one week after $208 vanished
Because Scott's family couldn't afford an Xbox
questions.hint: It's math suspicion, not eyewitness suspicion.
steps: Notice what Adam is doing: comparing the size of the money to the size of the explanation.
A brand-new console that 'you can't get in a store' costs far more than a kid earns doing chores — the story and the number don't balance.
Add the timing everyone knows: Evan's $208 disappeared the week before, at a party Scott left early.
But be precise about what this is: a reasonable doubt about Scott's story, not evidence of theft. Nobody saw anything — Adam included.

ex.main: **The story doesn't cover the amount.** The boys are doing real reasoning — explanations have to fit the size of what they explain. It's genuinely suspicious. It's also still not proof, which is the book's favorite trick.
ex.tip: 'That story doesn't add up' is legitimate evidence-weighing. Just keep it in a different pocket from 'I saw it happen.'

questions.q: Mid-scene, Jessie realizes she should have talked to Evan before serving the warrant. Why does her plan cost Evan more than it costs her?
opts: Because Evan wrote the warrant himself
Because Evan will have to pay if they lose
Because Evan is younger and more easily embarrassed
Because Evan is the victim, has to face these boys at recess every day, and will have to testify against Scott himself
questions.hint: The book lists Evan's burdens in one paragraph, right as Jessie realizes it.
steps: Find the moment: Scott turns to Evan — 'Are you saying I stole your money?' — and suddenly the case isn't Jessie's paper, it's Evan's word.
The book spells out Jessie's realization: Evan was the victim, Evan has to play with Scott at recess every day, Evan will have to testify in court.
Jessie can organize the trial and walk away; Evan lives inside it — his friendships, his daily recess, his credibility are the stakes.
And notice Evan's choice: three dribbles to think, then 'That's what I'm saying' — he backs her anyway, out loud, in front of everyone. Whatever it costs.

ex.main: **It's his money, his friends, his testimony.** Jessie built the trial, but Evan has to live in it — every recess, every day. Her realization ('she should have talked to Evan first') is the chapter's real lesson about acting FOR someone without asking them.
ex.tip: When one character acts on another's behalf, tally who actually carries the consequences. That gap is where authors hide their point.

questions.q: Why is it a big deal that it's "the fourth day of fourth grade for both of them"?
opts: They are twins who were separated before
Their school just opened
Jessie skipped a grade — so the little sister now sits in her big brother's class
Evan was held back a year
questions.hint: One of them isn't the usual age for fourth grade.
steps: The line quietly tells you something unusual: brother AND sister, same grade, same class.
Jessie skipped third grade — she is younger (still eight), has no bike license, and now shares Evan's room, teacher and friends.
That arrangement caused the lemonade war last summer; now it means every playground event happens in front of both of them.
Keep it in mind during the trial: the sibling dynamic is always in the courtroom too.

ex.main: **Jessie skipped a grade into Evan's class.** One quiet phrase carries the whole sibling setup — and explains why Jessie's fairness campaign happens on Evan's turf.
ex.tip: When a book states something odd very casually, it is trusting you to notice. The casual ones are load-bearing.

questions.q: The chapters run: Fraud, Revenge, Eyewitness, Hearsay, Accused … Trial by Jury … and finally Amends. What does the table of contents promise?
opts: The conflict will be handled like a real court case — and end not with winning, but with making things right
Each chapter is a separate story about a different crime
The trial happens in chapter one and the rest is aftermath
The book is secretly a law textbook
questions.hint: Read the titles as a path. Where does the path end?
steps: Read the titles in order: they trace a real case — the wrong, the anger, the evidence types, the accusation, the trial itself.
Now look at the final title: Amends — making up for a wrong. Not 'Verdict', not 'Winner'.
That ending word is a promise: whatever the jury decides, the story's real finish line is repair.
This is why the contents page is worth reading in any book — authors sign their intentions there.

ex.main: **A court-shaped story that ends in repair.** Sixteen legal terms in trial order, closing on Amends — the author tells you the destination before page one, if you look.
ex.tip: A patterned table of contents is a free prediction machine. Check your predictions against it as you read.

questions.q: The last chapter is titled 'Amends.' To make amends means:
opts: To win the argument
To get even with someone
To forget the whole thing happened
To make up for a wrong you did
questions.hint: It's the same idea as 'atonement' — the word already in the signed agreement.
steps: Amends is about repair: doing something real to make up for harm you caused.
Check it against the impostors: winning is about you, getting even is revenge (chapter 2's word), forgetting fixes nothing.
The kids already used the idea themselves — they signed an 'Agreement of ATONEMENT,' which is amends by another name.
Making amends requires admitting the wrong first — which is why it makes such a heavy final-chapter title.

ex.main: **To make up for a wrong you did.** Amends is repair plus responsibility — the exact opposite of revenge, which is where the book started. Chapter 2 to chapter 16 is the whole journey.
ex.tip: First and last chapter titles often argue with each other. Revenge → Amends is this book's argument in two words.
